newsitem.title: USA: Mississippi governor vetoes school funding bill.
newsitem.headline: Mississippi governor vetoes school funding bill.

text.p: Mississippi Gov. Kirk Fordice said Friday he has vetoed a bill that changed the way the state funds public schools because it could have caused budget shortfalls and encouraged excessive bond debt.
Fordice said he would call a special legislative session on April 23 to revamp the Adequate Education Act (SB2649). Lawmakers could also override the veto with a two-thirds vote.
Fordice acted minutes before a midnight Thursday night deadline to sign or veto bills or allow them to become law without his signature.

The proposal would have used general fund surpluses and new revenues to raise school spending by $12 million to $14 million annually, giving every county school system an eight percent increase over six years.

It also set a per-student minimum for spending, to be determined annually by the average per-pupil cost in districts recognized for high acheivements. For 1998, it would have been $2,664. Districts that could not meet that level would have been subsidized by the stae.

Fordice said the bill relied too heavily on increased revenues from economic growth that might not materialize and that it would be "very foolish" to assume Mississippi's economy would continue to grow at the current high rate.
"The full cost is too ill-defined," Fordice said. "How high the total cost of the program would be in later years is anybody's guess."
"The high cost of the program could very well result in future budget shortfalls," Fordice said in his veto message.

The bill also contained a provision allowing local school districts to assume up to $160 per student of new bond debt without a local referendum before June 30, 1998, or to refinance existing debt. In either case, the state would have been required to guarantee the debt.
"If every school district were to take us up on this offer, we would face an increase in bond debt of almost $1 billion," Fordice said.

He said it was "unrealistic" that would happen. But he said the proposal would have forced the state to guarantee bond obligations that were not approved by local taxpayers, the State Bond Commission or the Legislature.
"We should not encourge excessive bond debt by our school districts," Fordice said.
Fordice also said there was no guarantee that simply raising spending would produce a better education.
